catalog_quote: Stress, or accent, is not contrastive in Khatso at the word level. That is, there are no minimal pairs that are distinguished purely by different lexical stress patterns. Evidence for this conclusion is presented below. ... Unlike Putonghua, pitch is not a correlate of stress in Khatso. Because contours in different registers are already part of the lexical tone system, changing register alters meaning. ... An analysis of 90 disyllabic and trisyllabic responses obtained through elicitation, which include single as well as multiple word responses, fails to produce a predictable pattern involving the two features at the lexical level. ... None of the differences correlate with a specific lexical feature – segment, tone, syllable shape, syllable weight and word class are all irrelevant. ... new_statements.quote: Stress, or accent, is not contrastive in Khatso at the word level. That is, there are no minimal pairs that are distinguished purely by different lexical stress patterns. [...] As a result, the three features most likely to be used in lexical stress – pitch, intensity and duration – are not assigned at the word level in Khatso. Manipulating the pitch range of tone contours alters meaning, and thus is not an option for marking lexical stress. The remaining features, intensity and duration, pattern separately and, most importantly, randomly at the word level. Taken together, the evidence indicates that stress is not part of lexical phonology. Intensity and duration are used as IU boundary cues, however

new_statements.rule_in_words: Khatso is a tone language (eight lexical tones on every syllable) with no word-level stress: pitch is fully committed to lexical tone, and measured intensity and duration show no consistent word-level pattern across 90 elicited di-/trisyllabic tokens from two speakers. Prominence phenomena are phrasal: the intonation unit has an intensity peak on its first syllable and marked lengthening (lag) of its final syllable; 'Stress appears to be assigned at the phrase level rather than at the word level' (p. 140).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; no lexical stress of any degree is posited.
new_statements.exceptions: None at word level. Author notes elicited citation forms show final-syllable lengthening, but demonstrates (noun vs noun+classifier) that lengthening targets the last syllable of the phrase/IU, not of the word; intensity peaks may fall on the first syllable of a syntactic constituent or a pragmatically emphasized element within longer IUs (sec. 2.6.4).
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly word-level negative statement backed by acoustic measurements of elicited forms; phrase/IU-level cues described separately (IU-initial intensity, IU-final lag). Same analysis restated in Donlay 2021 ICSTLL-54 slides ('Khatso does not have lexical stress') and, per the author's site, revised into Donlay 2019 A Grammar of Khatso ch. 4 (not opened).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Khatso as spoken in Xingmeng 兴蒙 township (the single Khatso-speaking community), Tonghai County, Yunnan = Glottolog kats1235 / ISO kaf (Katso, Kazhuo 卡卓/喀卓, Gazhuo 嘎卓); no dialect split. Fieldwork 2012-2014.

sources.note: 'Khatso does not have lexical stress'; intensity acts independently as an IU cue, typically high at IU start; pitch-based IU cues (boundary tone, reset, tune) not used.
